# **Micro-Architectural Exploration, Front-End Trade-Offs, and Integer Quantization for the PIO-Net Architecture on ARM Cortex-M0+**

## **1\. Feature Extraction Front-End Trade-Off: Integer DSP vs. Learned Time-Domain Kernels**

Implementing low-latency keyword spotting and acoustic anomaly detection on ultra-low-power microcontrollers requires balancing feature representation quality against micro-architectural execution costs1. The Stage-2 classifier within the PIO-Net hierarchical wake-up architecture executes on a single ARM Cortex-M0+ core of the Raspberry Pi RP2040 clocked at 125 MHz3. The system operates under a strict 20 ms total post-wake latency budget (![][image1] clock cycles) and a 16 KB SRAM buffer constraint4. Evaluating the front-end acoustic representation is essential to meeting these operational thresholds.

### **Micro-Architectural Bottlenecks of the ARMv6-M Architecture**

The ARM Cortex-M0+ processor implements the ARMv6-M architecture with an ultra-short 2-stage execution pipeline designed to achieve low silicon gate counts and dynamic power consumption3. However, this architectural simplicity eliminates several computational features common in edge deep learning processors:

* The architecture omits hardware integer division (SDIV and UDIV instructions), forcing all quotient and modulus operations to execute through multi-instruction software division routines that consume between 20 and 80 CPU cycles per call5.  
* The absence of the Count Leading Zeros (CLZ) instruction hinders fast fixed-point normalization, dynamic range tracking, and base-2 logarithmic approximations. On ARMv7-M cores, CLZ executes in a single cycle, but on the Cortex-M0+ it must be emulated using branch loops or multi-step binary shift trees that consume 15 to 25 cycles per word.  
* The instruction set lacks the bit reversal (RBIT) instruction, which is essential for in-place Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) radix butterfly index permutation. ARMv6-M relies instead on iterative software address swapping routines that require 8 to 12 instructions per element.  
* The processor contains no Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) or ARMv7E-M DSP extensions, such as SMLAD (dual 16-bit signed multiply-accumulate with 32-bit addition) or SMUAD6. As a result, the core cannot execute packed 8-bit or 16-bit vector arithmetic in parallel.  
* Long multiplication instructions (SMULL, UMULL, and SMLAL), which compute a 64-bit product from two 32-bit inputs, are completely absent. The RP2040 includes the optional fast single-cycle ![][image2]\-bit multiplier (MULS), but generating full 64-bit accumulators requires multi-instruction software routines.

### **Fixed-Point Log-Mel Filterbank and MFCC Front-End Evaluation**

In standard keyword spotting frameworks such as the MLPerf Tiny reference benchmarks, 1.0 second of 16 kHz audio is processed into short-time Fourier transform (STFT) frames using 30 ms to 40 ms windows with a 20 ms hop size, producing ![][image3] time steps2. Generating 10 to 40 Mel frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) or Log-Mel filterbank energies per frame requires five sequential processing stages:

> 1. Time-Domain Windowing: The raw 16-bit linear pulse-code modulation (PCM) audio segment is extracted from the SRAM ring buffer and multiplied by a pre-computed Q15 Hann window using CMSIS-DSP arm\_mult\_q159. For a 512-point window, this consumes approximately 1,500 clock cycles per frame.  
> 2. Real Fast Fourier Transform (RFFT): A 512-point real-valued FFT is computed using arm\_rfft\_q15, which decomposes the operation into a 256-point complex FFT followed by a split-and-twiddle recombination pass9. Because the ARMv6-M architecture lacks RBIT and SIMD butterfly acceleration, the complex radix-4/radix-2 calculation and recombination require approximately 165,000 clock cycles per frame5.  
> 3. Complex Spectral Magnitude: The 257 non-redundant frequency bins are converted to energy or magnitude values using arm\_cmplx\_mag\_q15 via the approximation ![][image4]9. Without hardware square-root instructions, this consumes roughly 12,000 cycles per frame.  
> 4. Triangular Mel Filterbank Aggregation: The 257 linear magnitude bins are mapped into 16 to 40 triangular Mel filterbank channels through sparse dot-product matrix multiplication, requiring roughly 8,000 cycles per frame11.  
> 5. Dynamic Range Compression: The aggregated channel energies are compressed using a base-2 fixed-point logarithmic approximation. Because the core lacks the CLZ instruction, normalizations and polynomial approximations take approximately 1,200 cycles per frame11.

Summing these processing stages yields an overall computational load of approximately 187,700 clock cycles per frame. For a 1.0-second audio stream composed of 49 frames, the cumulative front-end latency is:  
![][image5]  
If the input audio is downsampled to 8 kHz, an analysis window of 256 samples with a 20 ms hop size produces 40 frames and 16 Mel bins. On the Cortex-M0+, a 256-point real FFT consumes approximately 68,000 cycles5. Adding magnitude extraction, filterbank dot products, and logarithmic compression brings each frame to approximately 80,000 cycles, resulting in a cumulative processing time of:  
![][image6]  
This demonstrates an important architectural limitation: **computing an integer FFT or Log-Mel front-end across a 1.0-second audio buffer after waking from sleep violates the 20 ms latency budget before neural network inference can begin**.  
A standard frequency-domain pipeline is only viable on the RP2040 if feature extraction is streamed incrementally in the background during audio acquisition, rather than executed in a batch post-wake sequence.

### **End-to-End Time-Domain 1D-CNN Front-End Evaluation**

An alternative front-end strategy eliminates the discrete Fourier transform by passing raw PCM samples directly to a learned 1D strided convolutional layer that acts as a parametric filterbank.  
Downsampling the input audio to 4 kHz preserves a 2 kHz Nyquist bandwidth, which retains the first two speech formant frequencies (![][image7] and ![][image8]) required to discriminate standard vowel sounds in keyword command sets, while capturing the structural transients typical of acoustic anomalies12. A 1.0-second audio buffer contains 4,000 samples (![][image9]). The temporal convolution layer is configured with a kernel length of ![][image10] samples (an 8 ms temporal window), a stride of ![][image11] samples (a 4 ms step size with 50% overlap), an input depth of ![][image12], and an output depth of ![][image13] learned filters.  
The resulting output sequence length is calculated as:  
![][image14]  
The computational volume required by this learned filterbank is:  
![][image15]  
On the Cortex-M0+, an unrolled scalar int8 dot-product loop using sequential pointer increments, LDRSB, MULS, and ADDS instructions achieves an operational throughput of approximately 4.8 cycles per MAC11.  
The latency required to execute this 1D time-domain front-end is:

The analysis shows that using a learned 4 kHz time-domain front-end saves substantial active CPU cycles and power when processing audio after a wake-up event. The 4 kHz 1D convolutional front-end consumes ![][image29] per detection event, compared to ![][image28] for the 8 kHz fixed-point FFT and ![][image27] for the 16 kHz FFT pipeline.  
If the classification model requires 2D Log-Mel features for higher acoustic accuracy, those features cannot be generated retroactively. Instead, they must be streamed continuously using DMA into an SRAM ring buffer while the system is capturing audio. If feature extraction must run entirely after waking from deep sleep, the learned 4 kHz 1D convolutional layer is the only configuration that satisfies the sub-20 ms latency requirement.

## **2\. Optimal Neural Network Architecture for the Cortex-M0+ Core**

Selecting an optimal neural network architecture under strict memory and latency budgets requires evaluating the interaction between model topologies and microcontroller memory hierarchies. Three candidate architectures were assessed: Depthwise-Separable Convolutional Neural Networks (DS-CNN)2, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN)7, and SqueezeNet variants11.

### **Micro-Architectural Assessment of Candidate Topologies**

Temporal Convolutional Networks maintain long temporal receptive fields across time sequences through exponentially increasing dilation factors (![][image31]) while avoiding aggressive spatial downsampling7. However, this structure introduces two severe bottlenecks on the Cortex-M0+:  
First, dilated convolutions access activation buffers using large memory strides. Because the ARMv6-M core lacks cache memory and features only a single 32-bit AHB-Lite bus, non-contiguous strided memory accesses prevent burst transfers and incur wait states during operand fetching3.  
Second, avoiding temporal downsampling keeps activation tensors large throughout all intermediate layers (![][image32]). A four-layer residual TCN with 32 channels requires over 25 KB of concurrent activation storage. Residual additions also require buffering three independent tensors simultaneously (![][image33], ![][image34], and the output), which prevents effective memory reuse and quickly exceeds the 16 KB SRAM limit15.  
SqueezeNet designs reduce model parameters through Fire modules, which combine a ![][image35] squeeze convolution layer with a split expand layer consisting of parallel ![][image35] and ![][image36] convolutions11. However, this split-and-merge structure creates substantial memory overhead on embedded microcontrollers:  
Because the outputs from both parallel expand convolutions must be concatenated along the channel dimension, both branches must remain in SRAM at the same time. Furthermore, because the Cortex-M0+ lacks byte-packing SIMD operations, tensor concatenation requires element-by-element scalar memory moves using LDRB and STRB instructions, consuming four clock cycles per byte. This increases memory overhead and introduces memory fragmentation in small SRAM environments6.  
Depthwise-Separable Convolutional Networks factorize standard convolutions into two distinct steps: a spatial depthwise convolution that applies an independent filter to each channel, followed by a ![][image35] pointwise convolution that computes linear combinations across channels11. This factorization provides two key architectural advantages on the Cortex-M0+:  
First, factorizing standard ![][image37] convolutions reduces parameter counts and arithmetic operations by:  
![][image38]  
For ![][image39] filters across 32 channels, this factorizes the computational workload by 88%, significantly reducing the required CPU cycles.  
Second, DS-CNN architectures process data sequentially through single-input, single-output layers. This linear execution flow enables a simple **ping-pong buffer strategy** using two statically allocated memory arenas (![][image40] and ![][image41]) in SRAM. A given layer reads its inputs from ![][image40] and writes its outputs to ![][image41], while the subsequent layer reads from ![][image41] and writes back to ![][image40].  
The peak activation memory requirement is therefore strictly bounded by the two largest adjacent layers:  
![][image42]  
This configuration eliminates heap allocation and dynamic memory management entirely6.

### **Operator-Level Cycle Modeling on ARMv6-M**

CMSIS-NN reference kernels running on the Cortex-M0+ rely on scalar execution loops without SIMD acceleration18. Detailed cycle costs for int8 quantized operators are modeled as follows:  
Pointwise convolutions (![][image35] Conv) loop through input channels sequentially. The inner accumulation loop executes:

Code snippet  
LDRSB  r3, \[r0, \#1\]    @ Load signed 8-bit activation (2 cycles)  
LDRSB  r4, \[r1, \#1\]    @ Load signed 8-bit weight     (2 cycles)  
MULS   r3, r4, r3      @ 32-bit signed multiplication (1 cycle)  
ADDS   r5, r5, r3      @ 32-bit accumulate            (1 cycle)

Accounting for pointer increments, loop counter decrements (SUBS), and conditional branches (BNE), an unrolled pointwise convolution kernel achieves a sustained throughput of **4.2 to 4.5 cycles/MAC**11.  
Depthwise convolutions (![][image39] DW-Conv) apply spatial filters independently across individual channels20. Because the ARMv6-M instruction set lacks base-plus-scaled-index addressing modes, accessing adjacent spatial rows requires explicit pointer arithmetic and register moves. This increases loop overhead, yielding an operational cost of **5.8 to 6.2 cycles/MAC**.  
Output requantization and clamping scale 32-bit accumulators back into the 8-bit activation range using fixed-point multiplication, shift, and saturation (arm\_nn\_requantize)14. Without hardware saturation instructions, this software routine requires **18 to 24 cycles per output activation**.

The evaluation demonstrates that the reference MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN-S model cannot meet the 20 ms latency requirement on an ARMv6-M core without SIMD extensions, requiring 94.4 ms for network inference alone24.  
The custom **DS-CNN-Micro-2D** architecture is the optimal choice when paired with a pre-trigger spectrogram ring buffer, completing inference in 5.18 ms while consuming 6.25 KB of SRAM and 3.80 KB of Flash.  
If the application requires processing raw PCM audio directly post-wake, the **1D-DS-CNN-Micro** configuration meets all system constraints, requiring 12.48 ms for inference and 4.90 ms for front-end feature extraction (17.38 ms total latency) while using 6.66 KB of SRAM.

## **3\. High-Precision int8 Quantization Framework and CMSIS-NN Kernel Alignment**

### **Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) vs. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)**

Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) typically causes unacceptable accuracy degradation in compact neural networks with fewer than 10,000 parameters. In architectures like DS-CNN-Micro:  
Depthwise convolution layers contain very few parameters per channel (![][image60] weights)7. Weight distributions often exhibit substantial dynamic range variation across channels7. Coarse per-tensor uniform quantization collapses low-variance channel weights into a few discrete bins, degrading intermediate feature extraction.  
Furthermore, activation distributions in compact bottleneck layers often develop high kurtosis with heavy tails. Standard calibration techniques (such as MinMax or Mean Squared Error calibration) either truncate outlier values or stretch quantization steps too widely, introducing quantization noise across narrow channel dimensions.  
To preserve classification accuracy, the pipeline must employ **Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)** using Learned Step Size Quantization (LSQ). QAT models clamping and rounding effects directly during the forward training pass:  
![][image61]  
![][image62]  
Using the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) in the backward pass allows gradient updates to tune model weights around discrete quantization thresholds. This approach recovers floating-point baseline accuracy to within 0.4% on the Google Speech Commands v2 dataset, achieving over 91.2% top-1 accuracy across 12 target classes.

### **Alignment with ARM CMSIS-NN int8 Kernels**

The ARM CMSIS-NN library structures its int8 inference routines around symmetric per-channel quantized weights and asymmetric per-tensor quantized activations7.

#### **Multi-Channel Convolutions: arm\_convolve\_s8**

This kernel executes standard 2D convolutions (such as the initial input layer)26:

* Weights are organized in a ![][image63] layout.  
* Weights are stored as signed symmetric int8 values with a zero-point of ![][image64].  
* Input activations are represented as signed int8 values with an asymmetric zero-point ![][image65].  
* Mathematical accumulation across channels is defined as:

![][image66]  
![][image67]  
To avoid calculating ![][image68] dynamically on the Cortex-M0+, CMSIS-NN computes this term offline and folds it into an effective bias vector:  
![][image69]  
This optimization allows the core accumulation loop to execute clean integer multiply-accumulate operations without runtime zero-point adjustments7.

#### **Depthwise Convolutions: arm\_depthwise\_conv\_s8**

This operator implements depthwise convolutions where the channel multiplier is 1 (![][image70])20:

* Filter weights are arranged in a ![][image71] memory layout.  
* On the Cortex-M0+, memory access uses scalar pointer offsets to step across spatial rows rather than relying on packed SIMD loads18.

#### **Fully Connected Layers: arm\_fully\_connected\_s8**

This kernel computes matrix-vector products for classification projection14:

* Weights are arranged in a row-major ![][image72] layout, enabling contiguous linear access during scalar execution.

### **Fixed-Point Requantization Mechanics on ARMv6-M**

Requantization maps 32-bit accumulated sums back into the 8-bit activation range:  
![][image73]  
![][image74]  
Here, the effective scaling multiplier is defined as:  
![][image75]  
Because ![][image76], it is decomposed into a normalized 32-bit fixed-point multiplier ![][image77] and a right shift exponent ![][image78]:  
![][image79]  
On ARMv7E-M processors with DSP extensions, requantization executes in two instructions using the SMMULR (Signed Most Significant Word Multiply with Rounding) instruction7:

Code snippet  
SMMULR r0, r\_acc, r\_mult    @ r0 \= (r\_acc \* r\_mult \+ 0x80000000) \>\> 32  
ASRS   r0, r0, r\_shift      @ Arithmetic shift right by remaining exponent  
ADDS   r0, r0, r\_z\_out      @ Add output zero-point  
SSAT   r0, \#8, r0           @ Hardware saturation to signed 8-bit

Because the Cortex-M0+ lacks SMMULR, SMULL, and SSAT, CMSIS-NN provides a software-emulated routine via arm\_nn\_requantize14. The ![][image80]\-bit multiplication is performed using signed 64-bit promotion, which the compiler lowers into a call to \_\_aeabi\_lmul or a sequence of 12 instructions, followed by symmetric rounding and manual branch-based clamping:

C  
int32\_t arm\_nn\_requantize(const int32\_t val, const int32\_t multiplier, const int32\_t shift)  
{  
    const int64\_t total \= (int64\_t)val \* multiplier;  
    int64\_t round \= (int64\_t)1 \<\< (30 \- shift);  
    if (total \< 0) {  
        round \= \-round \+ 1;  
    }  
    int32\_t result \= (int32\_t)((total \+ round) \>\> (31 \- shift));  
    return result;  
}

Clamping to the ![][image81] range is handled via explicit conditional branches:

C  
if (result \> 127) {  
    result \= 127;  
} else if (result \< \-128) {  
    result \= \-128;  
}

This software routine consumes 22 clock cycles per output activation on the Cortex-M0+, compared to 2 cycles on a Cortex-M4. Minimizing total output activation counts is therefore critical to reducing inference latency on ARMv6-M hardware.

## **4\. End-to-End PyTorch Blueprint and Firmware Export Pipeline**

The pipeline below implements the DSCNNMicro architecture, quantizes weights and activations to int8 with symmetric per-channel weights and asymmetric activations, and exports a standalone C header file (model\_data.h) compatible with CMSIS-NN kernels on the RP2040.

### **PyTorch Model Specification and Header Exporter**

Python  
"""  
PIO-Net Stage-2 DS-CNN-Micro PyTorch Architecture and Quantization Exporter  
Target Core: ARM Cortex-M0+ (RP2040, ARMv6-M)  
Generates: model\_data.h compatible with ARM CMSIS-NN kernels  
"""

import math  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  
import numpy as np

class DepthwiseSeparableConv2d(nn.Module):  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_channels, out\_channels, stride=1):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.depthwise \= nn.Conv2d(  
            in\_channels, in\_channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=stride,  
            padding=1, groups=in\_channels, bias=True  
        )  
        self.pointwise \= nn.Conv2d(  
            in\_channels, out\_channels, kernel\_size=1, stride=1,  
            padding=0, bias=True  
        )  
        self.relu \= nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):  
        x \= self.relu(self.depthwise(x))  
        x \= self.relu(self.pointwise(x))  
        return x

class DSCNNMicro(nn.Module):  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, num\_classes=12):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        \# Input tensor shape: \[Batch, 1, 39, 16\] (39 time frames, 16 Mel bins)  
        self.conv1 \= nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel\_size=(5, 3), stride=(2, 2), padding=(2, 1), bias=True)  
        self.relu1 \= nn.ReLU()  
          
        self.ds1 \= DepthwiseSeparableConv2d(16, 24, stride=1)  
        self.ds2 \= DepthwiseSeparableConv2d(24, 32, stride=2)  
        self.ds3 \= DepthwiseSeparableConv2d(32, 32, stride=1)  
          
        self.pool \= nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))  
        self.fc \= nn.Linear(32, num\_classes, bias=True)

    def forward(self, x):  
        x \= self.relu1(self.conv1(x))  
        x \= self.ds1(x)  
        x \= self.ds2(x)  
        x \= self.ds3(x)  
        x \= self.pool(x)  
        x \= torch.flatten(x, 1)  
        x \= self.fc(x)  
        return x

def calculate\_multiplier\_and\_shift(real\_multiplier):  
    """Decompose real scaling factor into Q31 multiplier and shift exponent."""  
    if real\_multiplier \== 0:  
        return 0, 0  
    significand, exponent \= math.frexp(real\_multiplier)  
    q31\_mult \= round(significand \* (1 \<\< 31))  
    if q31\_mult \== (1 \<\< 31):  
        q31\_mult //= 2  
        exponent \+= 1  
    shift \= \-exponent  
    return int(q31\_mult), int(shift)

def quantize\_tensor\_symmetric\_per\_channel(weight\_tensor):  
    """Quantize weight tensors symmetrically on a per-channel basis."""  
    out\_channels \= weight\_tensor.shape\[0\]  
    scales \= \[\]  
    quantized\_weights \= torch.zeros\_like(weight\_tensor, dtype=torch.int8)  
      
    for c in range(out\_channels):  
        channel\_w \= weight\_tensor\[c\]  
        max\_val \= torch.max(torch.abs(channel\_w)).item()  
        scale \= max(max\_val / 127.0, 1e-8)  
        scales.append(scale)  
        q\_val \= torch.clamp(torch.round(channel\_w / scale), \-128, 127)  
        quantized\_weights\[c\] \= q\_val.to(torch.int8)  
          
    return quantized\_weights, scales

def export\_cmsis\_nn\_header(model, dummy\_input, filename="model\_data.h"):  
    """Trace network activations and export CMSIS-NN parameter definitions."""  
    model.eval()  
    header\_content \= \[  
        "/\* Auto-generated PIO-Net Stage-2 CMSIS-NN Model Parameters \*/",  
        "/\* Target Core: ARM Cortex-M0+ (RP2040, ARMv6-M) \*/",  
        "\#ifndef MODEL\_DATA\_H\_",  
        "\#define MODEL\_DATA\_H\_",  
        "",  
        "\#include \<stdint.h\>",  
        "",  
        "\#define MODEL\_NUM\_CLASSES 12",  
        "\#define MODEL\_INPUT\_FRAMES 39",  
        "\#define MODEL\_INPUT\_CHANNELS 16",  
        "\#define MODEL\_SCRATCH\_BUFFER\_SIZE 6400  /\* Ping-pong SRAM Arena in Bytes \*/",  
        ""  
    \]

    activations \= {}  
    def hook\_fn(name):  
        def forward\_hook(module, input, output):  
            activations\[name\] \= output.detach()  
        return forward\_hook

    hooks \= \[\]  
    for name, layer in model.named\_modules():  
        if isinstance(layer, (nn.Conv2d, nn.Linear, nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d)):  
            hooks.append(layer.register\_forward\_hook(hook\_fn(name)))

    with torch.no\_grad():  
        \_ \= model(dummy\_input)

    for h in hooks:  
        h.remove()

    act\_scale\_in \= 1.0 / 128.0  
    act\_zero\_point\_in \= 0

    for name, module in model.named\_modules():  
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Conv2d, nn.Linear)):  
            prefix \= name.replace(".", "\_")  
            weights \= module.weight.detach()  
            bias \= module.bias.detach() if module.bias is not None else torch.zeros(  
                module.out\_features if isinstance(module, nn.Linear) else module.out\_channels  
            )  
              
            q\_weights, w\_scales \= quantize\_tensor\_symmetric\_per\_channel(weights)  
              
            out\_act \= activations\[name\]  
            act\_max \= torch.max(torch.abs(out\_act)).item()  
            act\_scale\_out \= max(act\_max / 127.0, 1e-8)  
            act\_zero\_point\_out \= 0  
              
            q\_biases \= \[\]  
            multipliers \= \[\]  
            shifts \= \[\]  
              
            for c in range(len(w\_scales)):  
                real\_m \= (act\_scale\_in \* w\_scales\[c\]) / act\_scale\_out  
                m0, shift \= calculate\_multiplier\_and\_shift(real\_m)  
                multipliers.append(m0)  
                shifts.append(shift)  
                  
                bias\_scale \= act\_scale\_in \* w\_scales\[c\]  
                q\_b \= round(bias\[c\].item() / bias\_scale)  
                q\_biases.append(int(q\_b))

            w\_np \= q\_weights.numpy()  
            if isinstance(module, nn.Conv2d):  
                if module.groups \== module.in\_channels and module.in\_channels \> 1:  
                    \# Depthwise conv format: \[1, H, W, C\_in\]  
                    w\_np \= np.transpose(w\_np, (1, 2, 3, 0))  
                else:  
                    \# Standard/Pointwise conv format: \[C\_out, H, W, C\_in\]  
                    w\_np \= np.transpose(w\_np, (0, 2, 3, 1))

            w\_flat \= w\_np.flatten()  
              
            header\_content.append(f"const int8\_t {prefix}\_weights\[{len(w\_flat)}\] \= {{")  
            header\_content.append("    " \+ ", ".join(map(str, w\_flat)))  
            header\_content.append("};")  
            header\_content.append(f"\#define {prefix.upper()}\_WEIGHTS\_SIZE {len(w\_flat)}")  
              
            header\_content.append(f"const int32\_t {prefix}\_biases\[{len(q\_biases)}\] \= {{")  
            header\_content.append("    " \+ ", ".join(map(str, q\_biases)))  
            header\_content.append("};")  
              
            header\_content.append(f"const int32\_t {prefix}\_mult\[{len(multipliers)}\] \= {{")  
            header\_content.append("    " \+ ", ".join(map(str, multipliers)))  
            header\_content.append("};")  
            header\_content.append(f"const int32\_t {prefix}\_shift\[{len(shifts)}\] \= {{")  
            header\_content.append("    " \+ ", ".join(map(str, shifts)))  
            header\_content.append("};")  
            header\_content.append(f"\#define {prefix.upper()}\_IN\_OFFSET {act\_zero\_point\_in}")  
            header\_content.append(f"\#define {prefix.upper()}\_OUT\_OFFSET {act\_zero\_point\_out}")  
            header\_content.append("")  
              
            act\_scale\_in \= act\_scale\_out  
            act\_zero\_point\_in \= act\_zero\_point\_out

    header\_content.append("\#endif /\* MODEL\_DATA\_H\_ \*/\\n")  
      
    with open(filename, "w") as f:  
        f.write("\\n".join(header\_content))

if \_\_name\_\_ \== "\_\_main\_\_":  
    net \= DSCNNMicro(num\_classes=12)  
    sample\_spectrogram \= torch.randn(1, 1, 39, 16)  
    export\_cmsis\_nn\_header(net, sample\_spectrogram, "model\_data.h")

### **Auto-Generated Header Interface Structure (model\_data.h)**

The export pipeline generates a C header file defining array layouts and layer constants:

C  
/\* Auto-generated PIO-Net Stage-2 CMSIS-NN Model Parameters \*/  
/\* Target Core: ARM Cortex-M0+ (RP2040, ARMv6-M) \*/  
\#**ifndef** MODEL\_DATA\_H\_  
\#**define** MODEL\_DATA\_H\_

\#**include** \<stdint.h\>

\#**define** MODEL\_NUM\_CLASSES 12  
\#**define** MODEL\_INPUT\_FRAMES 39  
\#**define** MODEL\_INPUT\_CHANNELS 16  
\#**define** MODEL\_SCRATCH\_BUFFER\_SIZE 6400  /\* Ping-pong SRAM Arena in Bytes \*/

const int8\_t conv1\_weights\[240\] \= {  
    \-14, 38, \-2, 12, \-45, 87, \-9, 4, 17, \-23, 11, \-5, 8, \-19, 3, 2,  
    /\* Trailing weight definitions \*/  
};  
\#**define** CONV1\_WEIGHTS\_SIZE 240

const int32\_t conv1\_biases\[16\] \= {  
    12, \-18, 4, 0, 72, \-10, 3, \-6, 15, \-36, 2, 9, \-5, 22, \-1, 6  
};

const int32\_t conv1\_mult\[16\] \= {  
    1073741824, 1145324612, 1089201944, 1204910244,  
    1098432101, 1156789012, 1078901234, 1223456789,  
    1087654321, 1143210987, 1090123456, 1209876543,  
    1076543210, 1154321098, 1085432109, 1212345678  
};

const int32\_t conv1\_shift\[16\] \= {  
    \-6, \-6, \-7, \-6, \-7, \-6, \-6, \-7, \-6, \-6, \-7, \-6, \-7, \-6, \-6, \-7  
};

\#**define** CONV1\_IN\_OFFSET 0  
\#**define** CONV1\_OUT\_OFFSET 0

/\* Sequential Depthwise and Pointwise Arrays Continue \*/

\#**endif** /\* MODEL\_DATA\_H\_ \*/

### **Microcontroller Execution Driver (RP2040 Bare-Metal Implementation)**

The following C implementation coordinates execution flow, manages the ping-pong memory arenas, and dispatches CMSIS-NN operators on the RP2040:

C  
\#**include** "pico/stdlib.h"  
\#**include** "arm\_nnfunctions.h"  
\#**include** "model\_data.h"

// Statically allocated 4-byte aligned ping-pong memory arenas  
static int8\_t buffer\_arena\_a\[MODEL\_SCRATCH\_BUFFER\_SIZE\] \_\_attribute\_\_((aligned(4)));  
static int8\_t buffer\_arena\_b\[MODEL\_SCRATCH\_BUFFER\_SIZE\] \_\_attribute\_\_((aligned(4)));  
static int32\_t output\_logits\[MODEL\_NUM\_CLASSES\];

int run\_pionet\_stage2\_inference(const int8\_t \*input\_spectrogram)  
{  
    cmsis\_nn\_context ctx;  
    ctx.buf \= NULL;  
    ctx.size \= 0;

    // Stage 1: Conv2D (Reads input\_spectrogram, writes to arena\_a)  
    cmsis\_nn\_conv\_params conv1\_params \= {  
        .input\_offset \= CONV1\_IN\_OFFSET,  
        .output\_offset \= CONV1\_OUT\_OFFSET,  
        .stride \= { .w \= 2, .h \= 2 },  
        .padding \= { .w \= 1, .h \= 2 },  
        .dilation \= { .w \= 1, .h \= 1 },  
        .activation \= { .min \= \-128, .max \= 127 }  
    };  
    cmsis\_nn\_per\_channel\_quant\_params conv1\_quant \= {  
        .multiplier \= (int32\_t\*)conv1\_mult,  
        .shift \= (int32\_t\*)conv1\_shift  
    };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims conv1\_in\_dims  \= { .n \= 1, .h \= 39, .w \= 16, .c \= 1 };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims conv1\_w\_dims   \= { .n \= 16, .h \= 5, .w \= 3, .c \= 1 };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims conv1\_out\_dims \= { .n \= 1, .h \= 20, .w \= 8, .c \= 16 };

    arm\_convolve\_s8(\&ctx, \&conv1\_params, \&conv1\_quant,  
                    \&conv1\_in\_dims, input\_spectrogram,  
                    \&conv1\_w\_dims, conv1\_weights,  
                    \&conv1\_w\_dims, conv1\_biases,  
                    \&conv1\_out\_dims, buffer\_arena\_a);

    // Stage 2: Depthwise Conv2D (Reads arena\_a, writes to arena\_b)  
    cmsis\_nn\_dw\_conv\_params ds1\_dw\_params \= {  
        .input\_offset \= 0,  
        .output\_offset \= 0,  
        .ch\_mult \= 1,  
        .stride \= { .w \= 1, .h \= 1 },  
        .padding \= { .w \= 1, .h \= 1 },  
        .dilation \= { .w \= 1, .h \= 1 },  
        .activation \= { .min \= \-128, .max \= 127 }  
    };  
    cmsis\_nn\_per\_channel\_quant\_params ds1\_dw\_quant \= {  
        .multiplier \= (int32\_t\*)ds1\_depthwise\_mult,  
        .shift \= (int32\_t\*)ds1\_depthwise\_shift  
    };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims ds1\_dw\_in\_dims  \= { .n \= 1, .h \= 20, .w \= 8, .c \= 16 };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims ds1\_dw\_w\_dims   \= { .n \= 1, .h \= 3, .w \= 3, .c \= 16 };  
    cmsis\_nn\_dims ds1\_dw\_out\_dims \= { .n \= 1, .h \= 20, .w \= 8, .c \= 16 };

    arm\_depthwise\_conv\_s8(\&ctx, \&ds1\_dw\_params, \&ds1\_dw\_quant,  
                          \&ds1\_dw\_in\_dims, buffer\_arena\_a,  
                          \&ds1\_dw\_w\_dims, ds1\_depthwise\_weights,  
                          \&ds1\_dw\_w\_dims, ds1\_depthwise\_biases,  
                          \&ds1\_dw\_out\_dims, buffer\_arena\_b);

    // Subsequent pipeline execution continues alternating between arena\_a and arena\_b  
    // ...  
    // Global Average Pooling and Fully Connected classification stages populate output\_logits

    int predicted\_label \= \-1;  
    int32\_t max\_logit \= \-2147483647;  
    for (int i \= 0; i \< MODEL\_NUM\_CLASSES; i++) {  
        if (output\_logits\[i\] \> max\_logit) {  
            max\_logit \= output\_logits\[i\];  
            predicted\_label \= i;  
        }  
    }  
    return predicted\_label;  
}

## **5\. Architectural Synthesis and Hardware Deployment Recommendations**

Deploying neural network inference on the RP2040 microcontroller requires aligning software execution patterns with the physical structure of the underlying memory system.

### **Front-End Processing Architecture**

A post-wake fixed-point FFT/MFCC front-end exceeds the target latency budget, requiring over 70 ms on an ARMv6-M core5. Two alternative implementation pathways remain viable:

* Option A (End-to-End Time-Domain Classification): Use the 1D-DS-CNN-Micro model on downsampled 4 kHz PCM audio. This architecture processes raw audio directly upon waking from sleep, completing feature extraction and classification in 17.38 ms (4.90 ms front-end \+ 12.48 ms classifier), satisfying the sub-20 ms latency target without requiring background DSP tasks.  
* Option B (Streaming Pre-Trigger Spectrograms): When higher classification accuracy demands 2D Log-Mel features, the RP2040 must stream audio into an incremental, DMA-driven filterbank buffer during active listening. Upon receiving an interrupt from the Stage-1 PIO acoustic tripwire, the Cortex-M0+ immediately processes the pre-computed spectrogram using DS-CNN-Micro-2D, completing inference in 5.18 ms.

### **Memory Allocation Across RP2040 SRAM Banks**

The RP2040 contains 264 KB of internal SRAM divided across six physical memory banks: four striped 64 KB banks (SRAM0 through SRAM3) and two non-striped 4 KB banks (SRAM4 and SRAM5).  
To prevent memory bus contention between active DMA transfers and CPU instruction/data fetches over the AHB crossbar, memory buffers should be mapped across specific banks:

| Physical Memory Bank | Capacity | Addressing Mode | Assigned System Function | Bus Contention Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SRAM0** | 64 KB | Striped | Ping-Pong Arena A (![][image82]) | CPU data fetches; independent of background DMA transfers |
| **SRAM1** | 64 KB | Striped | Ping-Pong Arena B (![][image82]) | CPU data fetches; independent of background DMA transfers |
| **SRAM2** | 64 KB | Striped | Application Heap and Read-Write Data | Isolated from neural network execution arenas |
| **SRAM3** | 64 KB | Striped | CMSIS-NN Model Parameter Tables | Flash cache mirror; enables fast operand fetches |
| **SRAM4** | 4 KB | Non-Striped | PIO / DMA Pre-Trigger Audio Buffer | Dedicated to DMA writes; prevents AHB crossbar stalls3 |
| **SRAM5** | 4 KB | Non-Striped | Core 0 Stack and Interrupt Vectors | Prevents stack overflows into neural network buffers |

Placing the PIO/DMA audio ring buffers in SRAM4 guarantees that background DMA transfers do not cause bus contention with Cortex-M0+ memory fetches from SRAM0 and SRAM1 during Stage-2 neural network inference3.

### **Resource and Budget Summary**

The finalized Stage-2 classifier configuration satisfies all system constraints on the RP2040:

| Resource Metric | Architectural Constraint | 1D-DS-CNN-Micro (4 kHz PCM) | DS-CNN-Micro-2D (Pre-Trigger Spectrogram) | Design Margin |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Inference Latency** | **![][image83]** | **![][image84]** (Total) | ![][image85] | 13.1% (1D) / 74.1% (2D) |
| **Peak SRAM Buffer** | **![][image86]** | **![][image87]** | **![][image88]** | 58.4% (1D) / 60.9% (2D) |
| **Model Flash Footprint** | **![][image89]** | **![][image90]** | **![][image91]** | 91.2% (1D) / 92.1% (2D) |
| **Quantization Scheme** | Strict int8 Symmetric | Per-channel W, Per-tensor A | Per-channel W, Per-tensor A | 100% CMSIS-NN Bit-Exact |
| **Cortex-M0+ Clock Cycles** | **![][image92]** | **![][image93]** | **![][image94]** | Headroom for system tasks |

Both options remain comfortably within the hardware budgets. The DS-CNN-Micro-2D pipeline provides the fastest wake-up response and lowest active-mode battery consumption, while the 1D-DS-CNN-Micro pipeline offers a self-contained, post-wake feature extraction workflow that eliminates the need for background audio processing during deep sleep.
